look_here_first: Look at the architecture: a tall plant with long bare internodes and an open candelabra-like panicle made of many short compact flower spikes; the leaves are simple, narrow, sharply serrate, and not lobed.

project_inclusion.range_basis: Kew/POWO accepts Verbena brasiliensis and gives its native range in South America; Texas is explicitly listed as introduced. TexasInvasives.org identifies Brazilian vervain as introduced to the U.S., reports it throughout central/east/north Texas, and describes it as a significant invasive species. NPSOT classifies Verbena brasiliensis as an invasive plant and notes its threat of displacing native plants. The project source pool contains seven user observations marked wild, supporting strong local encounter value but not native status.
project_inclusion.range_guardrail: Native status remains FAIL regardless of local abundance. Invasive comparison retention is a separate learner decision and is excluded from native totals.

best_field_traits: introduced South American annual or short-lived perennial, often 0.9–2.3 m tall
erect strongly 4-sided green stems with long internodes
opposite simple elliptic to oblanceolate leaves, sharply serrate above midblade
leaves sessile/subsessile and not deeply lobed
open panicle with several orders of opposite branching
many short compact terminal spikelets rather than a few long spikes
tiny violet-purple flowers and prolific small mericarps/seeds
morphology_keys.verbena_training: Tall open candelabra architecture + simple narrow serrate leaves + many short compact spikes separates this common invasive from local native Verbena.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Verbena scabra: V. scabra has broad harsh sandpaper leaves and very long slender spikes; Brazilian vervain has narrow simple serrate leaves and many short compact spikes in an open panicle. Verbena xutha: V. xutha has deeply 3-lobed leaves and coarse hispid/glandular foliage; Brazilian vervain leaves are simple and unlobed. Verbena bonariensis: A separate introduced ornamental/naturalized Verbena with dense rounded flower heads on long peduncles; do not collapse it into V. brasiliensis.
